item.title: Stock markets fall as Trump pivots from corporate meddling to fresh tariffs
item.description:
The duality of Trump has been on full display this week.

Yesterday, he helped stock markets by intervening to reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Today, he's preparing to announce new tariffs on China and dozens of other countries and that's weighing on markets.

The S&P 500 is down 1.1% and the Nasdaq lower by 2.1%.

The WSJ was earlier out with the scoop, and it says that the US will hit China, the EU and many other countries with tariffs due to industrial subsidies. That said, it's not a surprise, the Trump administration has been working to reconstruct its tariff regime on firmer legal grounds since the Supreme Court struck down its original tariffs in February. Notably, on Friday Jamieson Greer told Bloomberg that the subsidy investigation would be done very soon and certainly before year end. There has been talk since August that the US was looking to add an additional 7.5% tariff on China.

These levels wouldn't be a surprise as they would return to the status quo from 2025.

The surpris is that the administration intends to target most imports rather than only industrial sectors with demonstrable excess capacity and it has provisions for tariffs to rise further if foreign countries don't change industrial policies.

Now this isn't another Liberation Day but it's an inflationary move into a time when the Fed is already hiking. The market is priced for 26 bps in December and 58 bps through March. That's come in since the latest market volatility but this threatens to make inflation more sticky and hit consumers with tariff headlines just as they're getting ready to go Christmas shopping.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US broader stock indices give up some of the gains from yesterday with sellers remaining in control

Today, the indices are giving back some of those gains. That keeps the sellers in control for now. The levels that capped yesterday’s rebound are still the barometers for the next move. If the rally stalls below resistance again, the focus turns back to support and how much of yesterday’s bounce the buyers can defend.

item.title: Richmond Fed composite Index for November comes in higher at 3 versus -2 last month
item.description:
The Richmond Fed composite Index for the month of November comes in stronger at 3 versus -2 last month.

  • Richmond Fed manufacturing index — +3 vs −2 forecast. Prior −2.

November components vs October

  • New orders — +2 vs −8
  • Shipments — +2 vs 0
  • Employment — +6 vs +3
  • Local business conditions — +4 vs −8
  • Prices paid, 12-month growth — 7.59% vs 7.12%
  • Prices received, 12-month growth — 5.27% vs 5.27%

Fifth District manufacturing activity improved modestly in November, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond. The composite index moved back above zero after two months at −2. New orders led the rebound, while shipments and employment also improved.

The outlook firmed as well. Expected shipments rose to 28 from 19, expected new orders to 27 from 22, and expected employment to 13 from 8. Input costs grew faster, while selling-price growth held steady. Firms expect both rates to ease over the next 12 months.

The current condition components for November vs October sees MoM improvement, but inflation rises

  • Manufacturing index: +3 vs −2, up 5 points
  • Shipments: +2 vs 0, up 2 points
  • New orders: +2 vs −8, up 10 points
  • Order backlogs: −6 vs −21, up 15 points
  • Capacity utilization: 0 vs −7, up 7 points
  • Vendor lead times: +16 vs +18, down 2 points
  • Local business conditions: +4 vs −8, up 12 points
  • Capital expenditures: −10 vs −12, up 2 points
  • Finished goods inventories: +4 vs +4, unchanged
  • Raw materials inventories: 0 vs −2, up 2 points
  • Equipment and software spending: −9 vs −8, down 1 point
  • Services expenditures: −5 vs −19, up 14 points
  • Employment: +6 vs +3, up 3 points
  • Wages: +24 vs +20, up 4 points
  • Availability of needed skills: −10 vs −7, down 3 points
  • Prices paid growth: 7.59% vs 7.12%, up 0.47 percentage points
  • Prices received growth: 5.27% vs 5.27%, unchanged

Current conditions improved across most of the Richmond Fed’s November manufacturing survey. Of the 17 current readings, including the headline index, 12 rose, three fell and two were unchanged. The composite index rose 5 points to +3 from −2, with all three of its components improving. New orders led the way, rising 10 points to +2, while employment rose 3 points and shipments rose 2 points. Order backlogs posted the biggest gain, up 15 points, though they remained negative at −6. Services spending rose 14 points but also stayed negative, while local business conditions climbed 12 points to +4.

The weaker spots were equipment and software spending, which slipped 1 point to −9, and the availability of needed skills, which fell 3 points to −10. Vendor lead times accounted for the third decline, though the lower reading signals that delivery times lengthened less broadly. On prices, input-cost growth picked up to 7.59% from 7.12%, while selling-price growth held at 5.27%. Finished goods inventories were also unchanged.

The Expectation components also shows improvement with lower inflation expectations. 

  • Shipments: +28 vs +19, up 9 points
  • New orders: +27 vs +22, up 5 points
  • Order backlogs: +7 vs +7, unchanged
  • Capacity utilization: +10 vs +8, up 2 points
  • Vendor lead times: +14 vs +13, up 1 point
  • Local business conditions: +15 vs +7, up 8 points
  • Capital expenditures: −1 vs +4, down 5 points
  • Finished goods inventories: −3 vs +3, down 6 points
  • Raw materials inventories: −3 vs −3, unchanged
  • Equipment and software spending: +3 vs +2, up 1 point
  • Services expenditures: −9 vs −12, up 3 points
  • Employment: +13 vs +8, up 5 points
  • Wages: +44 vs +49, down 5 points
  • Availability of needed skills: −6 vs −7, up 1 point
  • Expected prices paid growth: 5.06% vs 5.32%, down 0.26 percentage points
  • Expected prices received growth: 3.82% vs 4.30%, down 0.48 percentage points

Expectations improved across much of the Richmond Fed’s November manufacturing survey. Of the 16 forward-looking readings, nine rose, five fell and two were unchanged. Expected shipments posted the biggest gain, rising 9 points to +28, while expected local business conditions climbed 8 points to +15. The outlook for new orders and employment also firmed, with both indexes up 5 points to +27 and +13, respectively. The expected availability of needed skills improved by 1 point but remained negative at −6.

Capital spending was the clearest weak spot, with the expectations index falling 5 points to −1 from +4 despite the stronger outlook for orders and shipments. Expected finished goods inventories fell 6 points to −3, and the wages index eased 5 points to +44. Firms also lowered their 12-month growth expectations for both prices paid, to 5.06% from 5.32%, and prices received, to 3.82% from 4.30%. Expectations for order backlogs and raw materials inventories were unchanged. The inflation guidance is good news. 

Quick analysis

The move back above zero is a modest positive for manufacturing, with new orders the component to watch for follow-through. Firmer demand and faster input-cost growth could lend some support to the US dollar and Treasury yields. Steady selling-price growth and expectations for easing price pressures limit what one regional survey is likely to change for the Fed.

What this report measures

The Richmond Fed’s monthly survey tracks shipments, new orders and employment at manufacturers in the Fifth Federal Reserve District. The seasonally adjusted composite is a diffusion index. A positive reading means improvement was more widespread than deterioration, and traders use it as an early regional read on factory demand and hiring.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US November consumer confidence 103.3 vs 92.5 expected
item.description:
• Prior was 91.7 (revised to 91.9)
  • Present situation 132.8 vs 120.4 prior
  • Expectations 83.6 vs 72.6 prior
  • The share of consumers saying jobs are “plentiful” minus the share saying jobs are “hard to get”—improved by 7.6 ppts to +12.4%.

This is a great rebound in a beaten-down series but likely reflects the politics that have infected everything and the passing of the midterms. Two months ago, the series was at the lowest since 2014. That said, last week's major retailer earnings and commentary was positive on the macro side.

Today, retail comps came in solid. Best Buy led at +6.1%, its best in five years and nearly triple the 2.3% consensus. Abercrombie was next at +6%, with every region accelerating, then Dollar Tree at +4.6% on 3.8% traffic growth and Kohl's at +1.2%, its first top-line growth in more than four years.

The macro read is less clean. Best Buy's blended ASPs rose 6% with units flat, and computing prices jumped 25% on memory costs while units fell mid-teens. That's goods inflation flattering nominal sales, and HPE says memory supply stays tight into H2 2028. Dollar Tree's traffic points to continued trade-down. Tariff refunds flattered margins everywhere and Dollar Tree is putting some of that money into lower prices, but none of it repeats in Q4. Best Buy's 2-4% Q4 comp guide says the pace is already cooling.

“Consumer confidence rallied again in November, potentially due to lower uncertainty following the midterm elections,” said Fergus McCormick, Senior Economist, Global Indicators, The Conference Board. “After two months of consecutive increases, the headline index is back to levels of confidence last seen in January 2025. The gain in confidence was led by stronger perceptions of present and future labor market conditions. Perceptions of current and future business conditions also improved sharply. Along with the gain in headline confidence, consumers planned slightly higher spending on goods and vacations.”

For background, the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index is released at 10 am ET on the last Tuesday of each month, making it the final major read on US household sentiment before the month closes. It's benchmarked to 100 in 1985 and is one of two headline sentiment gauges, alongside the University of Michigan survey.

The index combines consumers' views on current conditions with their outlook for the next six months. The Present Situation Index reflects how people assess business conditions and the job market today. The Expectations Index captures their outlook for business conditions, employment and household income six months ahead. The Conference Board has long noted that an Expectations Index below 80 has historically signaled a recession within the following year.

Its biggest distinction from the Michigan survey is a heavier focus on jobs. The most closely watched detail is the labor differential, the share of respondents who say jobs are "plentiful" minus the share who say jobs are "hard to get." It tracks the unemployment rate closely and often turns before the official labor data, which makes it a useful cross-check ahead of the monthly payrolls report.

The survey also covers 12-month inflation expectations, expectations for interest rates and stock prices, and plans to buy homes, vehicles and big-ticket appliances. Open-ended responses show what's weighing on consumers, whether prices, tariffs, politics or job security.

Confidence measures have a loose relationship with actual spending, and consumers frequently keep spending even when they report feeling gloomy. Markets usually react only to large surprises. The report's main value is in its labor market detail and in tracking how households are responding to inflation, gasoline prices and the jobs picture heading into the holiday shopping season.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin slips back below its old floor as sellers lean on $60,000.
item.description:
Bitcoin is back on the defensive after yesterday’s push above the old floor between $61,183 and $62,470 failed to hold. The price reached $64,570 before rotating lower into the close. The selling carried into today’s session, taking Bitcoin down to $59,321 before it bounced back toward $60,250. At that level, it is still down 1.52% on the day.

The price has been trading on both sides of $60,000. That round number will get attention, but the old floor just above it is the better barometer for the short-term bias. Yesterday, buyers got above the entire area and had a chance to build on the break. Today, sellers have pushed the price back below it. That puts the burden back on the buyers. In the video above, I take a outline the technicals behind my thinking and explain and show why.  

The old floor defines close risk for sellers

As long as the price stays below $61,183–$62,470, sellers can lean against that area on a bounce. A move above $61,183 would take the price back into the zone and give buyers a chance to chip away at the bearish bias. It would take a break above $62,470 that can hold to give buyers more control and open the door for a deeper correction.

If buyers can clear the zone, yesterday’s high at $64,570 would be the first upside target. Above that, the falling 100-bar moving average on the four-hour chart comes in at $66,458. The 38.2% retracement of the move down from the September 21 high is just beyond it at $67,417. Bitcoin fell below that retracement on November 14 and has stayed below it since. Getting back above the old floor would give buyers some breathing room, but those levels would still stand in the way of a broader recovery.

On the downside, $58,000 comes into view

If sellers take out today’s low at $59,321, the next target is the swing area near $58,000. Below that, the focus shifts to last Friday’s low at $55,081. A break there would take Bitcoin into territory it last traded in during early September 2024.

Below Friday’s low, the September 7 swing low at $52,546 and the October 4 swing low at $49,607 are the next historical references. The chart has a deeper 2024 reference at $39,531. There are several levels for sellers to get through before that last one comes into play, but the size of the decline puts those older levels back on the chart. At Friday’s low, Bitcoin was already down a little more than 56% from its October 2025 high of $126,272.

Below is the technical ladder for Bitcoin. The sellers are in control below the swing area. 

What traders can take from the failed break

An old floor can give traders a place to define risk after a failed break. Yesterday’s move above $62,470 gave buyers an opening. When the price slipped back through $61,183, sellers regained the advantage and got a nearby area to lean against. For now, watching how the next bounce behaves at $61,183–$62,470 can tell traders more than another trip back and forth across $60,000.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: November Belgian business confidence falls to the lowest of the year
item.description:
• Prior was -9.8

October had risen 2.3 points to -9.8, the highest since January and well above expectations of -11.8. November's 4.9-point slide more than reverses that, and you're back below the -12 to -13 range that held through the summer.

That puts the weak euro (near the lowest since April 2025) into perspective. The indicator has been negative since early 2022. Its long-run average since 1980 is about -7.3, with a record low of -36.1 in April 2020. Belgian business sentiment has spent nearly five years below normal, and this puts it in the bottom of that range.

It's a sign of a broader weakening in the economy. The eurozone composite PMI fell to a four-month low of 51.7 in October from 53.1 in September.

The National Bank of Belgium publishes its monthly business barometer, or business confidence indicator, near the end of each month, usually around 9 am ET. It's one of the earliest survey readings on European business conditions each month and has a long track record as a leading indicator for the broader eurozone economy.

The survey asks Belgian firms about current conditions and expectations across four sectors: manufacturing, construction, trade and business-related services. Responses are expressed as balances of positive and negative answers, seasonally adjusted. The headline is the overall synthetic curve, which combines the sector indicators. A reading above zero means confidence is above its long-term average, and a reading below zero means it's below. The NBB also publishes a smoothed version of the curve that strips out short-term noise and makes it easier to spot turning points.

The survey's macro value comes from Belgium's position in the European economy. It's a small, highly open economy deeply integrated into the supply chains of Germany, France and the Netherlands, with exports equal to a very large share of GDP. The port of Antwerp-Bruges is one of Europe's largest gateways for goods and chemicals, and Belgium has a major chemicals and pharmaceuticals industry. Because Belgian firms sit at many intermediate points in European production, shifts in their orders and sentiment tend to show up early.

Historically, turns in the Belgian barometer have often preceded turns in eurozone GDP and industrial activity, which is why some economists treat it as a bellwether for the euro area cycle. That makes it a useful early cross-check on the PMIs and Germany's Ifo survey and on the European Central Bank's growth outlook.

The report rarely moves markets, and the euro typically shows no reaction. Its value is as an early signal for European growth, particularly at turning points or when trade shocks such as US tariffs are hitting European manufacturers.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US September CaseShiller 20-city house price index +2.6 vs +2.7% expected
item.description:
• Prior was +2.7% y/y (revised to +2.6%)
  • Monthly index 0.1% vs +0.2% expected
  • Prior monthly was +0.3% (revised to +0.2%)

Data from the FHFA:

  • Prices y/y 2.5% vs +2.4% prior
  • Prices m/m 0.0% vs +0.3% prior

The US housing market is bad but it's not getting worse, despite rising interest rates.

For background, the S&P Case-Shiller Home Price Indices and the Federal Housing Finance Agency's House Price Index are the two main measures of US house prices. Both are released at 9 am ET on the last Tuesday of the month and carry a two-month lag, so the November reports cover September.

The Case-Shiller 20-City Composite is the most widely cited. It tracks single-family home prices across 20 major metropolitan areas, including New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Miami, Dallas, Phoenix, Seattle, Boston and Atlanta. S&P also publishes a 10-city composite, a national index and readings for each metro, which often show wide regional gaps. In recent years, the Northeast and Midwest have generally outperformed parts of the Sun Belt and West, where new supply has grown faster. Each monthly figure is a three-month moving average, which smooths the data but adds to the lag. Markets focus on the unadjusted year-over-year change.

The FHFA index covers homes bought with conforming mortgages purchased or guaranteed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. That makes it a better gauge of the mainstream market, since it excludes jumbo loans and most cash purchases, which skew toward high-end and investor buying. FHFA reports seasonally adjusted monthly changes and annual changes nationally, for nine census divisions and for states.

Both indexes use a repeat-sales method, comparing sale prices of the same homes over time. That controls for shifts in the mix of homes being sold, a weakness of median price measures like the one in NAR's existing home sales report. The two usually point in the same direction, though differences in coverage and weighting mean the size of the moves can vary.

Because the data are stale by the time they're released, neither report moves markets much. Their value is in tracking the long-run trend in home values, which drives household wealth and confidence. Mortgage rates, tight inventory and the lock-in effect have been the main forces shaping prices.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: What is a short squeeze and why can it trigger violent rallies?
item.description:
A short squeeze occurs when investors who have bet against an asset are forced to buy it back as prices move higher, accelerating the rally. It is essentially a feedback loop in which rising prices trigger additional buying, pushing prices even higher.

To understand how it works, imagine an investor who borrows shares of a company and sells them at $100, expecting the price to fall. The investor plans to buy them back later at a lower price, return the borrowed shares and pocket the difference.

However, if the stock moves higher instead, the short position starts generating losses. Unlike a traditional long position, where the maximum loss is limited to the initial investment, short positions have theoretically unlimited downside because there is no ceiling on how high a stock can rise.

As losses accumulate, short sellers may face margin calls or decide to close their positions to prevent further losses. To do so, they must buy back the shares they previously sold. This creates additional demand, pushing prices up further and forcing even more short sellers to cover.

This is what makes short squeezes so violent. The buying is driven not only by investors who want to own the asset, but also by traders who are forced to exit losing positions quickly. The resulting demand can become self-reinforcing, producing sharp rallies that are disproportionate to any improvement in fundamentals.

Short squeezes are often amplified by high short interest, excessive leverage and lower liquidity. When a large portion of the market is positioned on the same side, even a relatively small positive catalyst can trigger an outsized reaction.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Suckers' Rally 3.0? Nasdaq surges as Nvidia reinstates Huang following White House pressure
item.description:
The Nasdaq jumped 7% in pre-market trading yesterday, triggering a temporary trading halt after news that Jensen Huang had been reinstated as Nvidia CEO following pressure from the White House sent NVDA shares up more than 30%.

The argument for the stock market to recover all the losses and eventually reach new record highs is based on the idea that the recent weakness was driven by Huang's departure. Moreover, the White House's intervention implicitly signals that the administration will do everything in its power to keep the AI boom going.

I’m sympathetic to this view, but the selloff wasn't driven by Nvidia alone. Credit spreads had already been widening well before Huang’s scandal, driven by growth concerns stemming from a more hawkish Fed and prolonged US-Iran tensions. These two drivers haven’t changed one bit.

The dovish repricing we’ve seen in the past weeks has been driven by the selloff in the stock market that exacerbated growth concerns and brought down many commodities as well. It wasn’t because of an improvement in the inflation outlook. Therefore, if the stock market recovers, rate hike bets will return and give the Fed more confidence to keep tightening.

I think this is setting up to be Suckers' Rally 3.0. I would expect the market to make at least one more high before potentially selling off to new lows. Right now, the risk sentiment is somewhat better thanks to Nvidia, so the market would likely need a fresh bearish catalyst to roll over again.

Overall, the outlook for the Nasdaq remains neutral to bearish as we would need an end to the Iran war or a more dovish Fed to get a sustainable bullish trend.

item.title: Markets didn't stay down for long
item.description:
Jensen Huang returns as CEO and rejoins the board, just six days after Nvidia’s chairman ruled it out.

According to the company’s statement, the decision followed a series of discussions and meetings that convinced directors of Huang's sincerity and his ability to lead the company.

They also received input from “senior U.S. government officials” suggesting his return poses no threat to national security. The call from President Trump may have helped too.

Aside from the latter part, the story echoes what happened at OpenAI almost exactly three years ago. On November 17, 2023, Sam Altman lost his job after the company’s leadership questioned his candor, only to return as CEO days later under a newly reconstituted board. Interestingly, with a potential OpenAI IPO, the company's leadership stability and governance could become even more important to investors evaluating its long-term prospects.

Is the case closed?

Judging by Nvidia shares surging nearly 30% after the announcement, investors seem ready to put the scandal behind them and get back to betting on the AI boom. For Nvidia stock, the rally also highlights just how closely investor sentiment remains tied to expectations for AI-driven growth and the company's dominant position in the chip market.

In reality, however, the story might be far from over. With Democrats set to take control of both chambers of Congress early next year, pressure on Nvidia — and potentially the entire AI sector — could intensify.

By the way, Senator Charles E. Schumer already posted on X: “The Trump Administration’s rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act. Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing.”

On the other hand, calls for tighter restrictions on US chip exports to China are gaining momentum, while questions remain over whether the tech giants will ever recoup their multibillion-dollar AI investments. Thus, while Huang may be, the industry is still on shaky ground.

But could this just be a temporary rebound before the bubble bursts?

Not necessarily. Unlike during the dot-com bubble, today's AI giants have real products, real revenue, and real profits, even though some valuations are out of line.

If demand for computing power falls short of expectations, some companies could struggle to repay or refinance the billions they've borrowed to build AI infrastructure. That said, the fallout might not be nearly as severe.

Still, it's worth keeping an eye on the Fed's next moves. Any hint of further rate hikes could rattle markets again. And with tensions in the Middle East keeping inflation elevated, that scenario looks quite plausible.

 

This article was written by IL Contributors at investinglive.com.

item.title: German Ifo survey hints at a recovery in November but the ECB still can't get too comfortable
item.description:
• Germany November Ifo business climate index 90.6 vs 90.5 expected
  • Prior 90.2; revised to 90.1
  • Germany November Ifo current conditions index 89.4 vs 89.1 expected
  • Prior 88.8
  • Germany November Ifo expectations index 91.9 vs 92.0 expected
  • Prior 91.6; revised to 91.5

Well, at least Germany is giving the euro something to smile about to start the week. Business sentiment in Europe's largest economy continues to improve in November, with firms growing more upbeat about both their current situation and the outlook.

Of note, Ifo says that the improved situation points to a return to GDP growth in Q4. And that goes hand in hand with the encouraging PMI figures from yesterday, which showed a stronger expansion in German business activity even as France continues to struggle.

What also stands out from the latest survey result is that the improvement is being supported by businesses feeling better about how things are going now, rather than just pinning their hopes on a brighter tomorrow. So, that suggests there's a bit more substance to the recovery as a whole.

That being said, the broader European economic picture is still a rather awkward one at this point in time.

The euro area is dealing with 4% inflation while economic fortunes across the region are not exactly moving in the same direction. Germany might be finding its feet again but the ECB has to set interest rates for the entire bloc, not just its largest economy.

So yes, the German recovery does give policymakers a little more breathing room to fight inflation. However, raising interest rates to combat what is largely an energy-driven inflation shock also risks choking off the very recovery that we're beginning to see. And not only that, the economic situation in the likes of France for example is still leaving a lot to be desired.

While a potential December rate hike is definitely on the table, the question now isn't so much whether the euro area economy is recovering. Instead, it is how much monetary tightening that recovery can actually stomach.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold finds some relief as forced liquidations ease after Nvidia news boosts stock markets
item.description:
Gold spiked to the upside yesterday after the news of Jensen Huang being reinstated as Nvidia CEO triggered a strong rally in equity markets. The reaction kind of confirmed the view that gold has been under pressure due to liquidations caused by stock market losses.

To understand the mechanics, imagine that an investment fund holds stocks, gold and government bonds. Some stocks suddenly crash, and the fund suffers losses on leveraged positions. The fund may need to raise cash to meet margin calls, reduce leverage or satisfy investor redemptions. Rather than selling only the assets that caused the losses, it may sell whatever it can liquidate quickly. Gold is particularly useful in this situation because it is highly liquid and can be sold quickly.

The Nvidia news helped reset the sentiment, which got very bearish in the final part of last week. But it doesn’t really change the bigger picture. The Fed is still going to raise rates and how much will depend on the economic data and the stock market conditions.

The US-Iran stalemate is still ongoing, and the situation doesn’t look like it’s going to improve anytime soon, with Trump continuing to signal renewed military campaign in case negotiations fail.

For gold, it’s a tricky situation because it keeps getting smashed lower when the stock market falls on growth concerns and it’s also pressured when the sentiment improves because the US dollar and real yields get support from the hawkish repricing.

Looking ahead, gold will likely need support from a dovish repricing in interest rate expectations either from weaker data, dovish Fed commentary or an end to the Iran war. item.title: USD/JPY flirts with danger again as the 160.00 mark puts Japan intervention risks back in focus
item.description:
How many times can you poke the bear before it finally wakes up and bites? Well, dollar bulls appear to be keen on finding that out as USD/JPY starts to push toward the 160.00 level this week.

The dollar continues to hold its own even amid a broader improvement in risk sentiment, while elevated Treasury yields are hardly doing the yen any favours. But at these levels, I'd argue that getting the direction right is only half the battle.

Looking at the daily chart, buyers have already been turned away around the 160.00 level on a few occasions earlier this month, much like what we saw towards the start of September.

For now, the convergence of the 100-day (red line) and 200-day (blue line) moving averages around 158.75-90 provides a useful technical reference point. Holding above that region keeps buyers in the hunt, whereas a sustained break below both levels could quickly put sellers back in the driver's seat.

As for the upside potential, Goldman Sachs is essentially telling traders not to push their luck.

The firm believes Japan's MOF remains willing to intervene again, especially if USD/JPY buyers keep testing the limits above the 160.00 mark:

"We continue to believe that the MOF would intervene again if it deemed necessary, and the likelihood should increase as USD/JPY moves above 160 based on prior actions this year. That should keep yen vol low while broader USD pressures remain positive, as we expect investors to be reluctant to push USD/JPY to new highs, given the risk of intervention and recent signs of constructive shifts in other key domestic policies (e.g. monetary policy) that have tilted the asymmetry clearly towards a stronger yen."

The firm's trade preference is rather telling too, with Goldman Sachs continuing to favour shorting EUR/JPY instead. That allows for maintaining exposure to a stronger yen without directly betting against the dollar. As such, it also offers some protection against dollar-positive developments involving energy prices, bond yields and broader risk sentiment.

So, what would we be watching from here?

Besides the obvious technical hurdles, pay close attention to the speed at which USD/JPY advances and any escalation in verbal warnings from Tokyo. The 160.00 mark isn't necessarily a hard line for intervention but any quick and sudden moves beyond that could invite a rather different response from Japanese officials.

item.title: US dollar refuses to budge despite the risk-on bounce, so what's keeping it so strong?
item.description:
I guess someone forgot to tell the dollar that we're having a risk-on party again, even if it's just for a day or two.

The greenback even gained modest ground despite the euphoric mood that swept across broader markets yesterday. And that just added to the hot streak since the start of the month, in which traders had been working with a more dour risk mood for the most part.

And even with the more positive sentiment carrying over to today, major currencies are little changed. And if anything else, the dollar still looks the more poised of the bunch. So, what gives?

The charts continue to do the talking in part, with EUR/USD staring at the prospect of five straight weeks of losses.

The break below the 200-week moving average (blue line) added further selling momentum in the pair, which gave sellers the impetus to push under 1.1000 as well. There was a brief test of the figure level early on yesterday but not before further selling pressures piled on, though falling short of breaking the 61.8 Fib retracement level of the swing higher since 2025 at 1.0905. A break below that level would put sellers in an even stronger position this week, despite the switch in the market mood.

Besides that, the price action in USD/JPY is also telling as the pair moves back up above 159.00 now despite the threat of Japanese intervention hanging over. A return towards 160.00 would certainly make things uncomfortable for Tokyo officials again.

But zooming out to the broader dollar story, it is more fascinating as to how it is managing to find friends on both sides of the risk spectrum.

As markets are once again celebrating the AI trade, Adam pointed out an argument for structural dollar demand through what is essentially the rise of the chip-dollar. It's a straightforward viewpoint about where the money is flowing when companies around the world are throwing billions at AI infrastructure, computing capacity and US technology.

As counterintuitive as it might seem to traditional traders, a return of risk appetite could actually be another tailwind for the greenback; though only from this aspect.

I'm not saying we should throw the traditional risk-on, risk-off playbook out the window. However, I'd certainly be wary of using a rebound in equities as a reason alone to sell the dollar at this juncture. After all, things like Treasury yields and Fed rate expectations continue to remain important pieces of the puzzle - especially with inflation concerns still keeping the higher for longer narrative alive.

But if you're buying the euro or the yen purely on the premise that a recovery in equities should translate to a weaker dollar, then that assumption is one that I'd be a little more careful with. For all the excitement surrounding the comeback in stocks yesterday, the FX market evidently isn't exactly singing from the same hymn sheet.

I'd like to see the technicals among major dollar pairs snap back before putting much faith in a broader reversal in the currency. For now, the dollar isn't giving much away even on a good day for risk trades. Can you imagine what might happen if the mood turns sour again?

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold gets a bit of a lifeline but the technical damage runs deep, so what now?
item.description:
Amid the turn in broader market sentiment yesterday, gold is finding some reprieve after having come dangerously close to the $3,500 mark at the end of last week. The good news at least is that there's still some fight in the old yellow metal. But unfortunately for gold buyers, fixing sentiment on Wall Street and fixing a broken technical picture are two very different jobs.

Looking at the hourly chart, the latest bounce has twice run into trouble against the 100-hour moving average (red line). That is seen around $3,668 currently, with sellers continuing to lean on the key technical level to keep the near-term bias more bearish.

For buyers, getting above that would be the first big step in trying to turn things around. But even then, the 200-hour moving average (blue line) near $3,782 presents another major near-term hurdle. Until we start seeing those levels give way, sellers still have a relatively straightforward playbook to work with.

As for the bigger picture:

There is some encouragement in seeing buyers put up a fight near the $3,500 mark, with gold also nudging back above the 50.0 Fib retracement level of its rally from the 2022 lows near $3,609.

Just an aside, there's no right or wrong way to draw the Fib levels when we're taking such a long-view chart. It is very much a matter of preference. One can draw it starting from the September 2023 lows or even from the 2018 lows and there's nothing wrong with that. At this juncture, you can draw multiples and use them as key levels that traders might see interest in when dealing with any extended pullbacks or when leaning on certain levels to defend.

But either way, still do pay attention to the key psychological levels such as the one at $3,500. They are equally important when the technical selling hits hard and when stops are run down quickly as we saw last week.

Circling back to the gold chart above, let's not forget the significance of the break below the 100-week moving average (red line) just under $4,000. That marked the first serious breach of the technical level since 2023.

So, that puts into perspective just how long buyers have been in control of the gold market and how rewarding it has been to buy almost every meaningful dip during that period. But after such a phenomenal run, we're finally seeing some genuine signs of exhaustion. And that's not something that will likely be fixed by a couple of good days on Wall Street.

For now, the tug of war is back on. Should the $3,500 floor give way, the next major area of technical interest doesn't come in until around $3,000-$3,140, where the 200-week moving average (blue line) and 61.8 Fib retracement level come into play.

As you know me, I've been a strong advocate for dip buying in gold over the past decade. And that structural view has not changed even with the latest selloff. However, I'd much rather pay a little more for gold with some technical conviction behind the recovery than get caught up trying to catch a falling knife at the moment.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Wall Street catches Jensen Huang fever, but is this all a dead cat bounce?
item.description:
So, what'd I miss?

Talk about picking the right, or should I say the wrong time to go off on a little break, eh? I leave for a little over a week and come back to find Wall Street flirting with a bear market, only for Jensen Huang to pull off one of the most spectacular comebacks in recent history. What a time to be alive.

Nvidia shares surged by a whopping 31% yesterday following news of Huang's reinstatement as CEO and that helped the Nasdaq gain by 6.5% while the S&P 500 rallied by 4.7%. And just like that, Wall Street has rediscovered its appetite for all things AI in a Jensen-sational turn. Have investors really gotten rid of their Huang-over? Okay, I'll stop with the puns now. ;)

While the market turnaround yesterday was rather stunning, is having Huang back really enough to wash away all the negativity that has plagued markets over the last few weeks? Or are we looking at a classic case of a dead cat bounce?

For some perspective, the Nasdaq had fallen nearly 19% from its record high in October before yesterday's rebound. The steep drop on Friday also saw the index come close to a test of its 100-week moving average (red line), as seen above. Considering the beatdown that tech stocks have taken, I would argue that markets were already ripe for some form of relief rally. And Huang's return just happened to provide the mother of all excuses for traders to pull the trigger.

But now, where does this leave us in terms of the near-term technical picture?

Looking at the hourly charts for both the Nasdaq and the S&P 500, dip buyers have not exactly wrestled back control just yet. The rebound has put some distance against the Friday lows but there is still plenty of technical damage to repair.

The first step is to reclaim a push back above the 100 (red line) and 200-hour (blue line) moving averages, and we're still not seeing that shape up. As such, the rebound is impactful but not quite suggestive of a material turnaround in market sentiment just yet. Only a push back above the key near-term levels above would signal stronger technical confidence that dip buyers are genuinely rebuilding their exposure rather than traders simply scrambling to close out bearish bets.

Besides that, the fundamental problems haven't gone away either. Treasury yields remain elevated, inflation is still proving stubborn, and the questions surrounding the sustainability and profitability of AI spending are no less relevant today than they were a week ago.

So yes, Jensen Huang might be back in the driver's seat. However, he is not quite in the position to fix all of those issues.

The hype and euphoria may still reverberate as emotions continue to flow, but the other complication is that investors will have very little time to make sense of it all this week. US markets will be closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving before returning for an abbreviated trading session on Friday. During this holiday season, you would typically see thinner liquidity conditions and that could make for some rather exaggerated moves in either direction.

Markets love a good comeback story but one spectacular day doesn't undo several weeks of selling. The question now is can dip buyers build on yesterday's gains without another blockbuster headline to help them along. Until they make a more convincing case on the charts, there's still every chance that this will turn out as being another classic dead cat bounce.

Don't get me wrong. I love me some good euphoria and there's a lot of dip-buying opportunities across multiple markets right now. However, let's not go too far to think that Jensen Huang returning is the formula to fix the intense scrutiny on lab ARR. Then again, it's not to say that it never was created from thin air anyway.

In any case, the bottom line is just be careful out there and not to let emotions and FOMO override you in times like these. Go back to the basics. Manage and identify key risk levels to your trade and work from there. Take your time. There will always be another dip to buy. You don't have to risk it all just to chase one fleeting moment. Never forget that.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: Huang's return powers Asia's AI rebound
item.description:

  • Gold's road back to $5,000: four big banks bet on recovery, but the Fed sets the pace
  • BlackRock says markets overprice Fed hikes, sees two not three as energy shock fades
  • PBOC sets USD/ CNY central rate at 6.7111 (vs. estimate at 6.6757)
  • Singapore sees AI boom carrying 2026, but slower AI investment growth to weigh on 2027
  • Bank of Korea seen hiking to 3.25% this week, with one final move in early 2027
  • Analysts cheer Huang's Nvidia return but question the board's sudden U-turn
  • Singapore Q3 GDP jumps 6.1%, growth forecast lifted to around 6% as exports boom
  • NinjaTrader Bid/Ask data change: does it affect your indicators and Tick Replay?
  • Goldman says AI's next test is proving the economics, not the technology
  • Fed's Williams won't rule out back-to-back rate hikes as data drives the path
  • ANZ pulls first RBA rate cut forward to June 2027, sees three cuts by early 2028
  • Tokyo gets its first look at the Nvidia whiplash as Asia trades the Huang rebound
  • Goldman sees up to $15 trillion for AI infrastructure as spending spreads beyond Nvidia
  • Fed's Williams pins inflation on unusual factors, sees 2027 bringing it lower
  • Nvidia's Huang is back. Monday's rally leaves three big questions unanswered.
  • Jensen Huang is back in charge. Nvidia moves higher.
  • investingLive Americas market news wrap: Nvidia climbs 30% as Jensen Huang returns

Summary:

  • The Kospi jumped about 7% and the Nikkei nearly 4% as Huang's return to Nvidia revived the AI trade, led by SK Hynix and Samsung
  • Chinese stocks edged up from a 16-month low after record state ETF buying, while the Hang Seng slipped to its weakest since April 2025
  • JGBs rallied across the curve, with the 10-year yield down about 8bp to 2.70%, as Japan's flash PMI showed factories strong and services slowing
  • Fed's Williams left back-to-back hikes on the table, while BlackRock argued markets are pricing too many
  • The BOK is seen hiking to 3.25% on Thursday, and ANZ brought its first RBA cut forward to June 2027
  • Singapore's Q3 GDP grew 6.1%, and its 2026 forecast was raised to around 6%
  • Oil held near a three-month low as supply outweighed Hormuz risk, gold steadied above $3,600 and bitcoin slipped toward $60,000, and dipped under

Asian stock markets staged a powerful rebound on Tuesday as Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive revived the AI trade, with South Korea's Kospi jumping about 7% and Japan's Nikkei gaining nearly 4%. Chinese shares lagged despite record state support, while oil hovered near a three-month low and the day's central bank commentary kept the focus on how much further the Fed will tighten.

AI rebound lifts Asia

The rally followed Wall Street's best session since April 2025, after Nvidia's board unanimously voted to bring Huang back. Korea led the region. The Kospi climbed around 7% to about 5,040, recovering the 5,000 level, and the Kosdaq rose about 5%. Memory chipmakers did the heavy lifting, with SK Hynix up about 8.6% and Samsung Electronics up about 8.2%. The rebound came a day after Seoul said it was ready to activate a market stabilisation fund of about 10.8 trillion won.

In Tokyo, which reopened after Monday's holiday, the Nikkei rose about 4% to around 58,670 and the Topix gained about 2.5%. Analysts broadly welcomed Huang's return as removing a major source of uncertainty for the AI sector, although some questioned the credibility of Nvidia's board after its reversal a week after ruling out his comeback.

Chinese and Hong Kong shares were more subdued. The Shanghai Composite edged up about 0.5% to around 3,555, rebounding from a 16-month low hit on Monday, and the tech-focused STAR50 rose 2.5%. State-backed funds bought a record 90 billion yuan of ETFs on Friday and exchanges eased margin rules over the weekend. Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell about 0.5% to its weakest since April 2025, with an AI index giving up an early 6% gain. One fund manager said Huang's return would help Chinese firms in Nvidia's supply chain but would not ease US chip controls on China.

Japan: bonds and stocks rally together

Japanese government bonds rallied across the curve after the three-day weekend, with gains holding even as equities surged. The 2-year yield fell about 5 basis points to around 1.78% and the 10-year about 8 basis points to around 2.70%. The flash November PMI showed Japan's economy splitting in two, with manufacturing rising to 53.7 on the strongest export orders since 2018 while services growth slowed to 50.5. Business optimism fell to its joint-lowest since 2020, though S&P Global said stubborn price pressures continue to back expectations of a Bank of Japan hike in December. USD/JPY held near 159.

Fed: hawks and doubters

New York Fed President John Williams said inflation remains too high and that he would not rule out raising rates at consecutive meetings if needed, while describing recent price pressures as driven by unusual factors and calling 2027 a year of lower inflation. He said tech-sector volatility had not upended his positive outlook. BlackRock took the other side of the debate, arguing markets are pricing too many hikes. It expects a December move and one more in the first half of 2027, as the energy shock's boost to inflation reverses. US 10-year Treasury yields held around 4.90%, and US stock index futures edged higher.

Asia-Pacific central banks

A Reuters poll showed 32 of 34 economists expect the Bank of Korea to raise its base rate to 3.25% on Thursday, with a final hike to 3.50% seen by the end of the first quarter of 2027. ANZ brought forward its forecast for the first Reserve Bank of Australia rate cut to June 2027 from November, citing a weakening labour market, and now sees three cuts taking the cash rate to 4.10% by February 2028. AUD/USD was flat around 0.6630.

Singapore's economy grew 6.1% in the third quarter from a year earlier, well above the 5.4% advance estimate, and the government raised its 2026 growth forecast to around 6% on AI-related export demand. It expects growth to slow to 2.5% to 4.5% in 2027 as the pace of new AI investment moderates.

AI's bigger picture

Goldman Sachs estimated that $10 trillion to $15 trillion could flow into AI infrastructure over the next six years, with spending increasingly reaching memory, packaging and power beyond Nvidia, and said the AI debate is shifting from proving the technology to proving the economics. PIMCO said heavy AI borrowing by the largest tech companies has squeezed the gap between top-rated and lower-rated investment grade bonds to a record low, while the weakest junk-rated borrowers face recession-like refinancing stress.

Oil, gold and crypto

Oil held near a three-month low, with WTI just under $80 a barrel, as rising supply outweighed renewed risk in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran said three tankers hit mines. Deutsche Bank estimated an oversupply of 1.7 million barrels a day in October. Gold steadied above $3,600 an ounce after last week's 9% slide, as Goldman Sachs, UBS, Bank of America and Societe Generale all forecast a recovery in 2027 but differed on its timing. Silver fell more than 1% to around $42.70. Bitcoin slipped about 1.7% to around $60,300, while US derivatives regulators said exchanges and clearinghouses may count discounted bitcoin, ether and payment stablecoins toward their financial reserves. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
